title: Who skipped work for GTA VI? Dutch staff, young men, and US soldiers
content:
After 13 years of waiting, GTA VI finally went on sale on 19 November. Workers across Europe rushed to book the day off, many turning it into a four-day weekend. Meanwhile, Brussels is rethinking the rules for online games, from virtual currencies to child protection.

Grand Theft Auto VI, developed by Rockstar Games, arrived after two delays and countless internet jokes about things happening “before GTA VI”. The game takes players back to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida, modelled on Florida. But while it is set in America, the excitement is worldwide, with European gamers rearranging their schedules to play.

According to Remote, a global HR platform, annual-leave bookings for the release day were 32 per cent higher than for the same Thursday in 2025 worldwide, among employees on its platform. Several EU countries recorded increases, with the Netherlands leading the global ranking at 58 per cent, followed by Ireland at 50 per cent and Spain at 46 per cent. Portugal and Poland both recorded increases of 29 per cent, Italy 25 per cent and France five per cent.

title: Factory worker turned lawmaker: More money for industry is not a long-term solution for Europe
content:
Rudi Kennes fought to save Opel’s Antwerp factory before entering the European Parliament. Now, as lawmakers negotiate the Industrial Accelerator Act, the former factory worker and trade unionist wants guarantees that supporting European industry will also benefit its workers.

The Belgian lawmaker represents The Left in negotiations on the proposal as a shadow rapporteur. The Industrial Accelerator Act seeks to strengthen European production, making the debate over what qualifies as “Made in Europe” particularly important to him.

I do not think this will be a long-term solution for Europe. We might buy ourselves some time by giving the industry another few hundred million or billion euros. Structurally, though, I do not think that solves the problem.
— Rudi Kennes (Left/BE)

title: Can Europe stop bots from hijacking democracy without ending anonymity?
content:
One criminal network used 40,000 SIM cards to set up almost 50m fake online accounts. As Europe heads into a busy election year, lawmakers in Brussels are asking how to stop such bot armies without taking away people’s right to speak anonymously online.

With a string of national elections due across Europe in 2027, the stakes are rising. Fake accounts, coordinated disinformation campaigns, and online harassment are fuelling concerns across the EU. Yet lawmakers are divided over how to tackle manipulation without undermining anonymity and freedom of expression.

Bot farms and social media anonymity took centre stage in the European Parliament on 16 November. MEPs, Europol, and civil society representatives met at a hearing of the Special Committee on the European Democracy Shield (EUDS). They discussed how automated accounts distort political debate, amplify divisive content, and target public figures. What divided MEPs most was the line between anonymity and inauthenticity.

title: Treatment should not depend on postcode, says EP Vice-President Tilly Metz
content:
Accessibility is not only about wheelchairs, says Tilly Metz. The newly elected Vice-President of the European Parliament wants an institution everyone can follow. Speaking to EU Perspectives, she also called for fairer healthcare and steady support for Ukraine.

Tilly Metz (Greens/EFA/LUX) outlined her priorities for her new mandate as Vice-President of the European Parliament. Her agenda focuses on both the people working within the institution and those trying to engage with its work.

Ms Metz wants to tackle barriers that often go overlooked. Her vision ranges from making the Parliament’s communication clearer to creating a healthier workplace across its three locations in Brussels, Luxembourg, and Strasbourg. This includes mental well-being and a sense of safety at work. It also covers less obvious factors such as indoor air quality and the use of non-toxic cleaning products.

“When we think about accessibility, we often think about people in wheelchairs. But it’s not only about wheelchairs. It’s about people with all kinds of disabilities,” Ms Metz said.

title: Experts back EU advanced materials plan but warn of costly road to market
content:
Lighter aircraft, better batteries, and plastics made from plants. Europe is good at inventing new materials, less so at making them. Brussels’ new plan to change that wins praise. But it is not binding, and its success rests on national governments.

Advanced materials include things like lightweight composites used in aircraft and cars, new materials for batteries and magnets, and bio-based alternatives to conventional plastics. Engineered to have specific properties, they can make products lighter, stronger, more efficient, or more sustainable. On 18 November, the European Commission presented an agenda to turn Europe’s strength in research into industrial leadership in this field.

The Commission’s proposal for an Advanced Materials for Europe agenda sets three benchmarks for 2035: a 20 per cent increase in research and innovation investment, 20 per cent more EU-based start-ups and scale-ups, and more projects reaching higher levels of industrial deployment, all compared with 2023. It also calls on member states to coordinate research priorities and improve access to testing facilities, industrial scale-up, and skills.

title: EU farm reform sparks fears of unequal funding across Europe
content:
European farmers may receive uneven financial support during the next round of the EU agricultural policy. Regional leaders fear that changing the rules for funding may end up supporting wealthier countries while neglecting rural development.

Funding for EU farms would be tied to national and regional partnerships in the new policy. The European Commission believes that this would give member states the flexibility to support their rural areas with other EU policies.

But various concerns were brought up during a high level meeting in Brussels as EU officials, parliamentarians and regional leaders discussed the next version of the Common Agricultural Policy (2028-2034). Regional leaders have asked for more guarantees on funding as well as a greater role in decision making.

The reform suggests that national governments can have greater autonomy in organizing farm support. But regional authorities are concerned that they could lose control over decisions that influence local farmers.

“The region cannot be simply somebody who is giving its advice.”
— MEP Herbert Dorfmann (EPP/ITA)

title: Prevention lacks one thing to win over finance ministers. Hard numbers
content:
The average European worker misses almost three weeks of work a year through sickness. A new study puts the cost to the EU at up to €810bn annually, roughly four per cent of its GDP. Yet governments still pour most of their health budgets into treatment rather than prevention.

Europe is losing workers and economic potential to illnesses that could be prevented. Its ageing population adds to the strain on social security systems and public finances. That is why health experts and policymakers argue that governments need to look seriously at prevention, not just at ways to treat disease.

At a conference in the European Parliament, health experts and policymakers warned that governments do not collect all the data they need. Without it, they cannot calculate the full cost of preventable illness, including lost working days, early retirement, and reduced productivity. The real question is whether Europe can afford to keep treating prevention as a secondary issue.

title: Sea to sky: How the new Frontex fragments migrant surveillance
content:
Frontex, the EU agency for the control of European borders, has allocated over €1bn for aerial surveillance in 2018–2028. The funding is growing rapidly: from €12m in 2018 to over €330m for next year.

Aerial surveillance is crucial for interceptions. According to LIMINAL, at least 33,000 migrants faced return to Libya and Tunisia between 2018 and 2024. The returns, by the security forces of those two countries, enjoyed the support of Frontex. (LIMINAL is a laboratory of the University of Bologna that investigates intersectional mobility and border violence.)

Lorenzo Pezzani, the mastermind of LIMINAL, told EU Perspectives that Frontex’s reform “comes as absolutely no surprise”. However, one of the main concerns is how Frontex “is playing a significant role in pushing for or enabling the use of drones within European civilian space”. The hotspot is the Central Mediterranean sea.

title: Can lighter green rules get Europe’s space sector off the ground?
content:
Last year, the US attempted 181 orbital launches, China 92, and Europe just eight. Lawmakers now want to narrow that gap with the bloc’s first common space rules. These would cover satellite safety, cybersecurity, and the environment, with less paperwork for smaller players.

Europe’s space sector moved a step closer to a single rulebook on Thursday. The European Parliament’s Industry, Research and Energy Committee approved its position with 73 votes in favour, one against, and two abstentions. The legislation, which the European Commission proposed in June 2025, would establish the first common EU rules for companies launching satellites, operating spacecraft, or providing space services in Europe. Currently, 13 EU countries have their own space legislation.

title: Journalism could get its first EU budget. If AgoraEU survives the cuts
content:
Artists, independent newsrooms, and civil society groups are caught in a tug of war over EU money. Lawmakers want to boost the bloc’s culture and democracy programme by a quarter. A Council proposal would cut it by almost a third.

The money would go to culture, independent journalism, and civil society. On Thursday, two Parliament committees adopted their position on the 2028–2034 AgoraEU programme, calling for €10.72bn. They were the Culture and Education committee and the Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs committee.

It passed with 64 votes in favour, 17 against, and two abstentions. More than 1,500 amendments were tabled to the Commission’s proposal, with MEPs Emma Rafowicz (S&D/FRA) and Alice Kuhnke (Greens/SWE) serving as co-rapporteurs.

Before the vote, Ms Rafowicz welcomed the compromise reached after difficult negotiations, but warned that Parliament’s ambitions would depend on securing sufficient funding during talks with EU governments. “Everything that we’re defending will never come to light if the budget doesn’t meet the expectations of the programme,” she told MEPs.

title: Superbug infections up 72%: Can Europe’s new pharma reward turn the tide?
content:
Antibiotic-resistant infections are rising across Europe. The EU hopes a new financial incentive will bring more antibiotics to market. It is due to take effect within months, but regulators are still working out which drugs will qualify.

Antibiotic-resistant bacteria continue to spread across Europe. Bloodstream infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae increased by 72% between 2019 and 2025, according to figures published by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) on 18 November. The EU aims to reduce these infections by 5% by 2030.

Carbapenems are a class of antibiotics used to treat severe bacterial infections. The ECDC says this type of bacteria spreads in healthcare facilities and is “linked to a high mortality rate.”

“We are still behind with several of the EU’s 2030 targets to counter antimicrobial resistance,” ECDC Director Pamela Rendi-Wagner said.

The EU sets five targets for 2030 in a Council Recommendation adopted in June 2023, using 2019 as the baseline year.

title: ‘Industrial scale-up requires European financing’: Companies urge EU to save competitiveness fund
content:
More than 75 businesses, including EDF, 3M, Orano and PowerCo, are urging EU leaders to strengthen the proposed European Competitiveness Fund as negotiations over the bloc’s next budget enter a decisive week. They want more funding for clean industrial production and greater certainty for companies building factories and expanding new technologies.

In a joint letter, the signatories call for a €26.6bn increase to the fund, backing the additional funding proposed by the European Parliament. They want a substantial share directed towards industrial decarbonisation and the clean transition. EU leaders meet on 26–27 November to negotiate the 2028–2034 budget, after failing to reach agreement in October.

Achieving this industrial scale-up requires reliable European financing, and the EU Competitiveness Fund offers an opportunity to secure it.
— Lilian Schwich, cylib co-founder and co-chief executive
